1 Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle; and they were gathered together at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamped between Socoh and Azekah in Ephesdammim.123✦ 2 Saul and the men of Israel were gathered together, and encamped in the valley of Elah, and set the battle in array against the Philistines.45✦ 3 The Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side: and there was a valley between them.✦ 4 A champion out of the camp of the Philistines named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span6 went out.789✦ 5 He had a helmet of bronze on his head, and he wore a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of bronze.101112✦ 6 He had bronze shin armor on his legs and a bronze javelin between his shoulders.131415✦ 7 The staff of his spear was like a weaver’s beam; and his spear’s head weighed six hundred shekels of iron. His shield bearer went before him.161718✦ 8 He stood and cried to the armies of Israel, and said to them, “Why have you come out to set your battle in array? Give me a man22, that we may fight together!”23✦ 11 When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.24 12 Now David was the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem Judah, whose name was Jesse; and he had eight sons. He has surely come up to defy Israel. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine.”56✦ 33 Saul said to David, “You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him; for you are but a youth, and he a man57 of war from his youth.”58✦ 34 David said to Saul, “Your servant was keeping his father’s sheep; and when a lion or a bear came and took a lamb out of the flock,5960✦ 35 I went out after him, struck him, and rescued it out of his mouth. This uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God62.”63✦ 37 David said, “Yahweh, who delivered me out of the paw of the lion and out of the paw of the bear, will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go! 1 Now the Philistines fought against Israel; and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain on Mount Gilboa.1✦ 2 The Philistines overtook Saul and his sons; and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul.2✦ 3 The battle went hard against Saul, and the archers overtook him; and he was greatly distressed by reason of the archers.3✦ 4 Then Saul said to his armor bearer, “Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through and abuse me!” But his armor bearer would not, for he was terrified. Therefore Saul took his sword and fell on it4.5✦ 5 When his armor bearer saw that Saul was dead, he likewise fell on his sword, and died with him.6✦ 6 So Saul died with his three sons, his armor bearer, and all his men that same day together.7✦ 7 When the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley, and those who were beyond the Jordan, saw that the men of Israel fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned the cities and fled; and the Philistines came and lived in them.8✦ 8 On the next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.9✦ 9 They cut off his head, stripped off his armor, and sent into the land10 of the Philistines all around, to carry the news to the house of their idols and to the people.11✦ 10 They put his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth Shan.12✦ 11 When the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead heard13 what the Philistines had done to Saul,14 12 all the valiant men arose, went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth Shan; and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.15✦ 13 They took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fasted seven days.

↩ ✧ Variant. Goliath’s height. MT reads "six cubits and a span" (≈ 9 feet 9 inches / 2.97m). LXX (Codex Vaticanus) and the Dead Sea Scroll fragment 4QSama read "four cubits and a span" (≈ 6 feet 9 inches / 2.06m). Most modern critical reconstructions prefer the shorter LXX/4QSama reading as original — still very tall for the Iron Age (the average Israelite male was ~5’5"), but within the range of medical pituitary disorders. The MT reading appears to be a textual-tradition expansion. One of the clearest cases where Dead Sea Scrolls discoveries directly affect translation choices in modern Bibles.

SCRIP a small bag or wallet usually fastened to the girdle (1 Samuel 17:40); “a shepherd’s bag.” In the New Testament it is the rendering of Gr. pera, which was a bag carried by travellers and shepherds, generally made of skin (Matthew 10:10; Mark 6:8; Luke 9:3; 10:4). The name “scrip” is meant to denote that the bag was intended to hold scraps, fragments, as if scraped off from larger articles, trifles. [Reviewer: condense Easton's entry as needed.]

↩ ◇ Note. "Yahweh of Armies." Yahweh tz’va’ot — one of the Bible’s major divine titles, military and cosmic at once (the "armies" can be human armies, the celestial host, or both). David’s declaration inverts Goliath’s reliance on weaponry: "you come with sword and spear, I come in the name." The contrast is the chapter’s theological argument. The title Yahweh tz’va’ot appears 285 times in the OT, concentrated in Samuel-Kings and the prophets.

↩ ◇ Note. Jonathan and David. The text’s language — souls "knit together," "Jonathan loved him as his own soul," covenant of ’ahavah (love) and brit (covenant) — has been read across a range of interpretive traditions: as ancient Near Eastern covenant friendship, as political treaty using kinship language, and (more recent readings) as a same-sex bond. The Hebrew text neither asserts nor excludes a sexual dimension; the language exceeds what later categories can cleanly map. Both Jewish and Christian readers across history have largely read it as exemplary friendship; modern scholarship is divided.

↩ ◇ Note. The Jonathan-David covenant. The covenant binds the two men and their offspring forever. The provision becomes pivotal in 2 Sam 9, where David seeks out Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s surviving son, to honor the oath. The narrative is one of the OT’s clearest examples of personal covenant operating across generational lines, parallel to but distinct from the Davidic dynastic covenant.

↩ ◇ Note. "The Lord’s anointed." David refuses to kill Saul, even with Saul defenseless and even given the prophetic announcement of the kingdom-transfer. The principle — the anointed king’s person is sacred, even when the king is rejected — becomes foundational for later Davidic-messianic theology. The episode is set up as a moral test David passes; chapter 26 sets up an almost-identical scene to confirm the pattern. The principle is later weaponized politically (in 2 Sam 1, David executes the Amalekite who claims to have killed Saul) and theologically (the "anointed" / mashiaḥ trajectory toward NT christology).

↩ ◇ Note. Abigail. One of the few women in the OT whose intervention prevents David’s bloodshed (25:32–34, "your discretion has kept me from coming today to bloodshed"). Her speech (25:24–31) is one of the longest sustained speeches by a woman in the Hebrew Bible — combining theological argument, political acumen, and personal loyalty. After Nabal’s death she becomes one of David’s wives. The narrative places her — alongside Bathsheba, Tamar — in the small set of women whose agency materially shapes the Davidic story.

↩ ◇ Note. The medium at En-dor. Saul, who had earlier banned mediums (28:3) per Deut 18:11, now consults one in desperation. The séance produces what the text presents as Samuel’s actual ghost, who reiterates Saul’s rejection (28:16–19). The narrative is one of the OT’s strangest passages — necromancy unambiguously condemned in law, yet here it apparently works. Jewish and Christian commentary has split: the apparition is genuinely Samuel (most premodern readings), or a demonic impersonation (Tertullian, Augustine), or a literary device showing Saul’s state. Either way the chapter is the bleakest in the book’s portrait of Saul.

↩ ◇ Note. The death of Saul. Saul and three sons die at Gilboa in defeat. Saul’s suicide-on-the-sword is the OT’s most extended portrait of a tragic protagonist: chosen, anointed, rejected, gradually unraveling, dead by his own hand. 2 Sam 1 will give the alternate account from the Amalekite (likely a fabricator). Saul’s death prepares the dramatic structure of 2 Samuel — the long-foreseen kingship transfer to David, opened by his lament for the man who tried to kill him.

↩ ◇ Note. The book of Jashar. Second of two surviving references to this lost work (cf. Josh 10:13). David’s lament is preserved here as quotation from a separate poetic anthology — strong evidence that pre-canonical Israelite literary collections existed and were drawn upon by the biblical narrators. Other lost works the OT references include the Book of the Wars of Yahweh (Num 21:14), the Acts of Solomon (1 Kgs 11:41), and various royal annals. The OT is not the totality of ancient Israelite literature but a curated selection from a larger corpus.

↩ ◇ Note. David’s lament for Jonathan. The phrasing — "surpassing the love of women" — has occasioned the same range of interpretive traditions as 1 Sam 18:1, and again the Hebrew text neither requires nor excludes a sexual reading. The lament’s formal artistry (with the refrain "How are the mighty fallen") is one of the high-water marks of Hebrew poetry. The poem is striking for what it doesn’t say: nothing of Saul’s persecution of David, only honor for the dead king and unguarded grief for his friend.

↩ ◇ Note. David and Goliath. David’s response to Goliath frames the battle theologically: not as strength against strength but as the name of YHWH against the gods of Philistia. The Dead Sea Scrolls and the LXX preserve a textual tradition in which Goliath is four cubits and a span tall (about 6’6") rather than the MT’s six cubits and a span (about 9’9"). The textual variant matters: the LXX/4QSam-a tradition presents a larger-than-normal but humanly-possible warrior; the MT presents a giant.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Mashiaḥ (מָשִׁיחַ). First robust use of the term "anointed" for the king. David refuses to kill Saul because Saul is YHWH’s mashiaḥ — the messianic concept enters scripture through this restraint, not through promise. From mashiaḥ comes Greek christos, English Messiah/Christ. Every messianic theology in later Judaism and Christianity descends from the conviction David expresses here: the king is sacred because anointed.

↩ ◇ Note. The medium of Endor. One of the strangest narratives in scripture. Saul, who himself banished mediums, now consults one — and the dead Samuel actually appears. The narrator does not minimize: Samuel speaks, prophesies Saul’s death, and the next chapter delivers it. The episode raises every classical question about the boundaries of cultic legitimacy, the reality of necromancy, and the nature of the dead — questions the text deliberately leaves unresolved.

↩ ◇ Note. The oracular consultation. David’s first act after Saul’s death is to inquire of Yahweh — the verb (sha’al) carries cultic technicality, evoking the priestly oracle through the ephod (1 Sam 23:9, 30:7, where Abiathar carries it). The contrast with Saul is structural: Saul’s last act was consulting the medium of Endor (1 Sam 28), having lost access to Yahweh’s word; David opens his reign by re-establishing the legitimate channel. Hebron is chosen not by political calculation but by oracular instruction — the narrative insists that the kingdom is given, not seized. The pattern recurs through 2 Sam 5:19, 5:23: David inquires before each major military move, until ch 11, where he conspicuously does not.

↩ ◇ Note. The second anointing. David is anointed three times: privately by Samuel (1 Sam 16:13), publicly by Judah here, and over all Israel at Hebron (5:3). The three-stage pattern reflects historical realism — kingship in early Israel was built incrementally through tribal acclamation, not imposed by a single act. Hebron, the Calebite stronghold and Abraham’s burial place (Gen 23), gives the southern coronation deep ancestral resonance. David rules seven and a half years from Hebron before relocating north, a span that allowed Judah to consolidate around him while the Saulide dynasty unraveled in the north.

↩ ◇ Note. Mahanaim — the rival capital. Abner relocates Saul’s surviving son across the Jordan to Mahanaim, well outside Philistine reach but also outside the historic Saulide heartland of Benjamin. The choice is a tell: Saul’s territorial base is so compromised by Philistine pressure (the same defeat that killed Saul at Gilboa, 1 Sam 31) that the rump kingdom must shelter in Transjordan. Mahanaim — "two camps" — was the site where Jacob met Esau (Gen 32:2) and would later be David’s own refuge during Absalom’s rebellion (17:24). The narrative is already foreshadowing: the place where the failing king goes to hide will become the place where the successful king flees.

↩ ◇ Note. The combat at Gibeon. Abner’s proposal — twelve from each side fight before the watching armies — is a ritualized representative combat known across the ANE world and from the Iliad. The form was meant to settle a dispute without full-scale battle; here it spirals into general engagement when the twenty-four kill each other simultaneously and neither side has the moral pretext to withdraw. The site of "Helkath Hazzurim" ("the field of swords," or possibly "of flints") commemorates the bloodbath. The episode prefigures David vs. Goliath inverted: representative combat that fails to substitute for war, rather than succeeding.

↩ ◇ Note. Asahel’s death and the blood debt. Abner kills Asahel reluctantly, after twice warning him off (2:21–22) — using the butt-end of the spear, perhaps in an effort to wound rather than kill. The narrative carefully establishes Abner’s lack of malice, which becomes critical when Joab takes Asahel’s blood as the legal pretext to murder Abner in 3:27. ANE blood-vengeance custom (the go’el ha-dam, "redeemer of blood," Num 35:19) gave the next of kin the right to kill the killer — but only outside a city of refuge and with intent. Joab’s later act ignores both qualifications. The narrator is laying the legal track on which Joab will be condemned.

↩ ◇ Note. Abner’s plea. One of the great peace-cries in OT narrative: the soldier asking the soldier to call off pursuit before the violence becomes self-sustaining. The phrase "shall the sword devour forever" is theologically loaded — picturing the sword as a personified consumer, never sated, an image picked up by Jeremiah (12:12, 46:10) and embedded in apocalyptic literature. Joab’s grudging assent ("if you had not spoken, surely in the morning the people would have gone away") admits that war by inertia would have continued. The exchange marks the temporary end of phase one of the civil war; phase two will be fought not between armies but between commanders by treachery.

↩ ◇ Note. The Hebron sons. Six sons by six different wives in seven and a half years: a list of future trouble. Amnon (firstborn) will rape Tamar; Absalom will kill Amnon and rebel; Adonijah will attempt the throne against Solomon. The text inserts the genealogy at exactly this point — between Saul’s collapse and David’s consolidation — to show what David is building alongside the kingdom: a polygynous royal harem that will produce the dynastic crises of the rest of the book. Deut 17:17 had specifically forbidden the king to multiply wives; the verse is a quiet narrative indictment that pays out across the next twenty chapters.

↩ ◇ Note. Rizpah and the politics of concubinage. Possession of a deceased king’s concubine was a public claim on his throne — the convention is reflected in Absalom going in to David’s concubines on the palace roof (16:21–22) and in Adonijah’s request for Abishag (1 Kgs 2:13–25). Ishbosheth’s accusation against Abner therefore reads political, not moral: Abner is being charged with making a play for the kingship himself. Abner’s furious reaction (3:8–10) is the reaction of a man whose loyalty has been impugned at the level of the throne. Rizpah herself returns at 21:10 in one of the most haunting scenes in the book, guarding her sons’ bodies against scavengers — a portrait that gives the briefly-named woman lasting weight in the narrative.

↩ ◇ Note. Paltiel’s grief. One of the OT’s quietest, sharpest character vignettes. Paltiel — given Michal as wife by Saul after David’s flight (1 Sam 25:44) — has lived with her for years and now follows her in tears as she is taken back. Abner’s curt "go, return" cuts off the relationship without ceremony. The text registers his loss without comment, but the placement matters: this is a small private cost of David’s political reconsolidation, set in a chapter dominated by men’s strategic calculations. Whatever Michal’s coldness toward David at 6:20 will mean later, the narrator has already shown us where part of her heart had been.

↩ ◇ Note. Joab kills Abner. Joab takes Abner aside under pretext of private conversation and stabs him at the gate of Hebron — a city of refuge (Josh 21:13). The illegality is laid on three levels: a treacherous welcome (a violation of guest-friendship), an act outside the rules of blood-vengeance (Asahel was killed in regulated combat, not premeditated murder), and a killing inside a refuge city. David’s curse in 3:29 condemns Joab juridically; his lament (3:33–34) absolves the throne politically; but the narrative will hold the debt open until Solomon settles it (1 Kgs 2:5–6, 28–34). Joab’s competence is indispensable, his methods are unforgivable, and David lacks the political strength to remove him — the contradiction will run the rest of the book.

↩ ◇ Note. David’s lament for Abner. A short, formal couplet preserved as poetry: "Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound, your feet not put in fetters; as one falls before the wicked, so you fell." The poem performs three political functions at once: honoring the slain commander (essential for winning over Israel), distancing David from Joab’s act ("all the people understood that day that it was not of the king to kill Abner," 3:37), and signaling that political assassination is not the Davidic style. The lament’s craft — like the lament for Saul and Jonathan (1:19–27) — argues for David as a working poet, not just the patron of court poets, well before the Psalter tradition.

↩ ◇ Note. The lame heir. The narrator interrupts the Ishbosheth assassination story to give us Mephibosheth — Jonathan’s son, dropped by his nurse fleeing the news from Gilboa, lame in both feet from age five. The placement is no accident: the chapter is about the elimination of Saulide claimants (Ishbosheth murdered, Rechab and Baanah hoping for reward), and the parenthetical reminds us that one Saulide remains. Mephibosheth’s lameness becomes legally significant — physically disqualified from kingship, he is no political threat — and sets up David’s ḥesed in ch 9, where he restores Saul’s grandson at the royal table. The Saulide line will continue, but only as objects of Davidic mercy.

↩ ◇ Note. David’s policy on king-killers. David’s reasoning is consistent across both episodes: in 2 Sam 1:1–16, the Amalekite who claims to have finished off Saul is executed; here, Rechab and Baanah present Ishbosheth’s head expecting reward and are executed instead. The pattern is not personal squeamishness but a publicly enacted royal doctrine — the anointed king’s body is inviolable, and those who break that taboo for political profit are themselves disposable. The doctrine builds Davidic legitimacy through theatrical refusal: David becomes king without ever raising his hand against a Saulide, even by proxy. The political theater is calculated, but the principle (kingship as Yahweh’s prerogative, not the assassin’s) is genuinely held.

↩ ◇ Note. The household teraphim. The detail is theologically loaded: David’s wife — the king’s daughter — keeps a household idol large enough to substitute for a sleeping man in bed. The same Hebrew word (teraphim) describes Rachel’s stolen household gods in Gen 31:19, 30–35; the parallel pattern (woman conceals idol from a pursuing male authority figure, lies about her actions) is unmistakable. Either Michal owns the idol legitimately as part of normal Israelite household religion (so most modern scholarship; cf. Judg 17–18, where teraphim function alongside Yahweh worship), or the narrator is exposing the syncretism that runs through Saul’s court. The verse is one of the OT’s incidental but revealing windows on the gap between Deuteronomic ideal and lived Israelite religion.

↩ ◇ Note. The proverb’s second occurrence. The phrase appeared first at 10:11–12, when Saul prophesied with the Naioth band immediately after his anointing — there it framed his ecstatic seizure positively, as confirmation of his calling. Here, near the end of his arc, the same phrase frames a scene of public humiliation: Saul stripping naked, prophesying involuntarily, lying on the ground for a day and a night. The narrative bookends Saul’s reign with the proverb in deliberate inversion: same words, opposite meaning. The phrase becomes the OT’s standard idiom for unexpected reversal and for the destabilizing effect of prophetic possession (compare Num 11:24–29, where Eldad and Medad’s prophesying produces similar surprise). The chapter closes Saul’s effective tenure as king; he survives chapters more, but he never again controls a scene the way David does from 19 onward.

↩ ◇ Note. The bread of the Presence. The leḥem ha-panim (literally "bread of the face") was the twelve loaves placed weekly in the sanctuary (Lev 24:5–9), reserved for priestly consumption. Ahimelech’s decision to give it to David and his men crosses the cultic line for a humanitarian one — and Jesus cites this exact episode in the synoptic Gospels (Mark 2:25–28, Matt 12:3–4, Luke 6:3–4) as the textual ground for his disciples’ Sabbath grain-plucking. The Davidic precedent becomes Jesus’ paradigm for the principle that ritual law yields to human need ("the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath"). The chapter that doomed the priests of Nob (ch 22) thus also became the OT episode most quoted in early Christian theology of law and mercy.

↩ ◇ Note. The feigned madness at Gath. David, fled to the Philistine city of Gath itself (Goliath’s hometown!), is recognized and feigns insanity to escape — scribbling on the gate, drooling on his beard. The episode is unflattering by design: Israel’s anointed-future-king reduced to a public spectacle in enemy territory, surviving by performance. The superscription of Psalm 34 attaches to this episode ("a psalm of David, when he changed his behavior before Abimelech") — an attribution that gives the apparently humiliating scene a devotional afterlife. The narrator’s point is not the king’s heroism but his vulnerability: at this moment David is what Mephibosheth will later be (lame at the king’s table) — a man surviving on his protectors’ tolerance.

↩ ◇ Note. The slaughter at Nob. Doeg the Edomite — a non-Israelite court official — executes eighty-five priests when Saul’s own bodyguards refuse the order. The episode is the OT’s starkest portrait of state-sponsored cultic violence by an Israelite king, surpassing in horror anything earlier in the canon. Three things mark its theological weight: the killers are non-Israelite mercenaries (the king’s own troops have a moral line they will not cross), the victims are priests of Yahweh wearing the linen ephod, and one survivor (Abiathar) escapes to David carrying the ephod that will function as David’s oracle through the rest of the book. Saul’s rejection by Yahweh, prophesied in chs 13 and 15, becomes an institutional and moral fact in this chapter. Psalm 52 is traditionally attached to this episode, addressed to Doeg. The shedding of priestly blood is the unredeemable charge that marks the end of the Saulide regime in moral terms long before it ends militarily.

↩ ◇ Note. Abiathar and the ephod. The lone survivor of the Nob massacre flees to David with the priestly ephod — the divinatory instrument used for casting the Urim and Thummim (cf. Exod 28:30, Num 27:21). David thereby acquires institutional access to oracular consultation in a way Saul has lost (cf. 28:6, "Yahweh did not answer him by dreams or by Urim or by prophets"). The Saulide regime has lost legitimate cultic apparatus; the Davidic court-in-exile has it. Abiathar will serve David as priest until Solomon dismisses him in 1 Kgs 2:26–27 — explicitly described there as fulfillment of the curse on Eli’s house (1 Sam 2:31–35). The Nob slaughter, the ephod’s transfer, and Abiathar’s eventual dismissal form one continuous narrative thread spanning the books of Samuel through 1 Kings 2.

↩ ◇ Note. The third covenant — and the last meeting. David and Jonathan’s third recorded covenant (cf. 18:3, 20:16–17) and the final scene the two share. Jonathan crosses Saul’s sphere of authority to find David in hiding — a politically dangerous act, since failure of the search-party Saul has dispatched is then explained by Jonathan’s warning rather than incompetence. Their parting words assign the future plainly: "you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you" (23:17). The pledge will not be kept, since Jonathan dies at Gilboa (31:2), but the underlying loyalty drives David’s long-term faithfulness to Mephibosheth (2 Sam 9). The scene is the closing frame of one of the OT’s most theologically rich friendships, registered with characteristic narrative restraint: the text gives no farewell speech, only the geographic separation that becomes permanent.

↩ ◇ Note. The women’s song. The victory chant is the immediate trigger of Saul’s decline — he hears the comparative figure (one thousand vs. ten thousand) as a public verdict that David is the better king, and his murderous resentment dates from this verse forward (18:9, "Saul kept watching David from that day on"). The poetic form — antiphonal women’s celebration of male victors — is the same form preserved in Miriam’s song (Exod 15:20–21), Deborah’s song (Judg 5), and the welcome of Jephthah’s daughter (Judg 11:34). The song will return as a haunting refrain in 21:11 and 29:5, twice quoted to David in Philistine territory by Achish’s men, where it functions inversely — the same words that menaced Saul now testify to David’s reputation in enemy ears. The song’s theological function is to register David’s rise as public fact before any narrative event yet confirms it.

↩ ◇ Note. The bride-price gambit. Saul demands an unpayable bride-price hoping David will die in the attempt — a classic ANE narrative motif (cf. Bellerophon and the Chimaera in the Iliad, Hipparkhia’s tasks in Mesopotamian tradition) inverted: the king who tries to kill the hero through impossible task is overcome by the hero’s success. Hebrew bride-prices typically involved silver or livestock (Gen 34:12, Deut 22:29); Saul’s demand for foreskins is theological and political — proof of dead Philistines combined with a humiliating violation of the enemy dead, since circumcision was the marker of covenant identity (Gen 17). David doubles the price (200 foreskins, 18:27), an act of reckless devotion that secures the marriage to Michal but seals Saul’s view of him as a threat the throne cannot absorb. The episode foreshadows the Bathsheba pattern decades later: David’s sexual-political ambitions producing collateral death.

↩ ◇ Note. Saul’s outburst. The insult is cast at Jonathan but functionally aimed at his mother Ahinoam (1 Sam 14:50) — and through her at the maternal lineage that produced an heir more loyal to David than to Saul. The phrase is among the most personal eruptions of rage in OT narrative; Saul ends the speech threatening to throw the spear at Jonathan as he had earlier thrown it at David (20:33, cf. 18:11, 19:10). The outburst is theologically diagnostic: Saul has come to read Jonathan’s loyalty to David not as a moral problem (which Jonathan is openly trying to address) but as a familial betrayal — a paranoid frame that the rest of the chapter shows is well outside political reality. By chapter’s end Jonathan has crossed from his father’s house in spirit; only his death at Gilboa will complete the separation in fact.

↩ ◇ Note. The cave of Adullam. David’s first base of operations as a fugitive — and the foundational site of his irregular military force. The verse following (22:2) describes those who gathered: "everyone who was in distress, in debt, and discontented." Four hundred men (later six hundred, 23:13) form a paramilitary band of socially marginal Israelites, the sociological core of what will later become David’s royal guard and the original "mighty men" listed in 2 Sam 23. The political significance is sharp: the Davidic regime is built first from below, by the disaffected and dispossessed of Saul’s kingdom, before it ever assumes formal power. The pattern — a king whose original constituency is the marginal — runs through Davidic theology and is picked up explicitly in NT framings of Jesus’ early followers (Matt 11:28, "all you who are weary and burdened"). The cave itself, located in the Shephelah, was a natural refuge frequently attested in subsequent guerrilla warfare in the same terrain.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Tz’ror ha-ḥayyim (צְרוֹר הַחַיִּים). "The bundle of the living" — Abigail’s phrase for the secure existence of those preserved by Yahweh, contrasted with souls "slung out as from a sling’s pocket." The image is concrete: a bundle (tz’ror) is a pouch in which valuables are tied for keeping; Yahweh keeps the lives of the faithful as a man keeps his treasure. The phrase enters Jewish liturgical tradition as one of the great eschatological formulas: titztzor bi-tz’ror ha-ḥayyim ("may [his/her soul] be bound up in the bundle of the living") is the standard inscription on Jewish gravestones to this day, and the Hebrew acronym תנצב"ה (T-N-Tz-B-H) on virtually every Jewish tombstone abbreviates this verse. Few biblical phrases have had so durable a liturgical-funerary afterlife.

↩ ◇ Note. Exile as forced apostasy. David articulates a theological principle of Israelite religious geography: to be driven from Yahweh’s land is, functionally, to be told "go, serve other gods" (26:19). The premise — that Yahweh’s effective worship is bound to Yahweh’s territory — is shared widely across early Israelite religion (cf. Naaman taking earth from Israel back to Aram, 2 Kgs 5:17) and only later modified by the exilic prophets (Jer 29, Ezek 11) into a theology of Yahweh present in exile. Davidic complaint here, on the cusp of his actual flight to Philistine Gath, registers the agony of forced removal from cult-territory in terms the post-exilic reader of Lamentations and Psalm 137 will recognize. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest articulations of the territorial dimension of pre-exilic Yahwism.

↩ ◇ Note. David’s double game. While taking refuge under Achish of Gath, David systematically raids the southern tribes — Geshurites, Girzites, Amalekites — leaving no survivors who could report his activity, then tells Achish he has been raiding Judah and its allies (27:10–12). The deception serves three ends: he protects Achish’s trust, he weakens Israel’s southern enemies (which will pay off when he becomes king), and he distributes the spoil to Judah’s elders (30:26–31), building political support for his eventual return. The narrative does not moralize the deceit; it presents it as the political competence that distinguishes David’s exile from Saul’s. The Amalekite raids in particular complete unfinished business from ch 15 — Saul lost his kingship for sparing Amalekites, David secures his by exterminating them. The strategic asymmetry is the chapter’s argument.

↩ ◇ Note. The Philistine commanders’ veto. The Philistine military council overrides Achish’s personal trust in David, refusing to let an Israelite war-band march in their formation against Saul. The narrative move is providential rescue dressed as political prudence: David is spared the catastrophic dilemma of either fighting his own people at Gilboa or betraying his Philistine patron. The commanders’ phrase — "let him not go down with us to battle, lest he become an adversary (Hebrew satan) to us" (29:4) — is one of the OT’s background uses of the term that will eventually be theologized as "the Adversary" of Job and later apocalyptic. Here the word means simply "battlefield turncoat." David’s gracious-sounding protest at being excluded (29:8) reads, at the level of plot, as the protest of a man who has been saved from an impossible situation by other people’s skepticism.

↩ ◇ Note. The law of equal shares. David’s ruling — that the two hundred who guarded the baggage at Besor receive an equal share of the recovered spoil with the four hundred who fought — becomes formally codified in 30:25: "he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel, to this day." The principle reverses common ANE military practice (combatants outranking support troops) and grounds itself in Yahweh’s gift theology: the victory was not earned by the combatants alone but given by Yahweh to the whole company (30:23). The ruling has long been read as the OT’s closest analogue to wages-of-the-laborers economics, anticipating the principle of Matt 20:1–16 (the workers in the vineyard, all paid the same regardless of hours). The verse is a small but theologically potent text in early Israelite military and economic ethics.

↩ ◇ Note. The Jabesh-Gileadites’ retrieval. The men of Jabesh-Gilead retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons from the Philistine wall at Beth-Shan, cremate them, and bury the bones — an unusual procedure (cremation is generally not standard Israelite practice; cf. 2 Sam 21:12–14, where the bones are later re-buried in Saul’s ancestral tomb in Benjamin) likely undertaken because the bodies were too desecrated for normal burial. The act closes a long-running narrative arc: Saul’s first major military victory was the rescue of Jabesh-Gilead from Nahash the Ammonite (ch 11), and these are the same people now risking themselves to honor their dead deliverer. The chapter ends not with Saul’s defeat but with this gesture of remembered loyalty — the small kindness that frames the failed king’s death is the gratitude of the people he saved at his beginning. David will explicitly bless them for it (2 Sam 2:5–7).

↩ ◇ Note. The tardēmah from Yahweh. The Hebrew tardēmah ("deep sleep") is the same rare word used of the divinely-induced sleep that fell on Adam at the creation of Eve (Gen 2:21) and on Abraham at the cutting of the covenant (Gen 15:12). The vocabulary signals to the reader that David’s second sparing of Saul is providentially staged: Yahweh, not luck, makes the entire camp sleep through David and Abishai’s incursion. The narrative architecture is deliberate — chapters 24 and 26 are doublets, paired demonstrations that David refuses to harm Yahweh’s anointed even when offered the opportunity. The earlier scene relies on geographic accident (Saul enters the cave where David is hiding); this one relies on supernatural sleep. The doubling makes David’s restraint structural rather than incidental, foundational to the political-theological argument the books of Samuel are building about the legitimacy of his eventual kingship.

↩ ◇ Note. The crisis of Davidic faith. The verse is one of the rare windows the narrative gives into David’s interior life, and what it shows is theologically jarring: after the two miraculous sparings of chs 24 and 26, after Samuel’s anointing, after every prior demonstration of Yahweh’s preservation, David concludes that he will eventually be killed by Saul and decides on his own initiative to seek refuge among the Philistines. The decision contradicts everything the narrative has been arguing about David’s exceptional providential protection. Robert Alter and others read the verse as a deliberate portrait of faith’s failure under prolonged stress — the pious protagonist of chs 24 and 26 collapses into the political pragmatist who will spend sixteen months as a Philistine vassal (27:7). The narrator offers no judgment, but the structure of the book (David’s subsequent absence from the Gilboa battle by Philistine veto, ch 29) implicitly registers it: human despair occasions the providential rescue that David does not manage for himself.

↩ ◇ Note. The song’s third appearance. The same verse the women sang in 18:7 — that triggered Saul’s descent into murderous resentment — now reappears in the mouths of Philistine commanders as the reason David cannot be trusted in battle alongside them (cf. its second appearance at 21:11, also in Philistine territory). The narrative pattern is theologically pointed: a song that began as celebration of Israelite victory has become so widely-known that even the enemy has internalized it as canonical fact. David’s reputation, established by women’s song outside political channels, has become the public truth Saul could not silence and the Philistines must now act on. The triple repetition of the same Hebrew couplet across three chapters with three different rhetorical functions (celebration, threat, military veto) is one of the OT’s clearest examples of a single textual fragment doing extended structural work in a narrative.

↩ ◇ Note. The pivot at Ziklag. The verse is the moral hinge of David’s exile period and one of the OT’s great formulations of leadership under collapse. Returning to find Ziklag burned, families captured, and his own men talking of stoning him, David does not respond with the strategic pragmatism of ch 27 or the despair of 27:1 — he strengthens himself in Yahweh his God. The verb (ḥazaq, "to make oneself strong") is the same one Yahweh uses repeatedly with Joshua (Josh 1:6, 7, 9, "be strong and courageous"). David then immediately consults the ephod (30:7–8) — the legitimate oracular channel he has had access to since 23:6 but did not use during the Philistine sojourn. The verse marks David’s return to the providence-trusting mode that defined chs 23–26 and exited at 27:1. The pivot is what allows the entire reversal of fortune in 30:18–20 to be theologically intelligible: not luck, not strategy, but the king’s recovery of his proper posture toward Yahweh.

MAON habitation, a town in the tribe of Judah, about 7 miles south of Hebron, which gave its name to the wilderness, the district round the conical hill on which the town stood. The First Book of Samuel 17:1.

Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and were gathered together at Shochoh, which [belongeth] to Judah, and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וַיַּאַסְפ֨וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֤ים אֶת־מַֽחֲנֵיהֶם֙ לַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וַיֵּאָ֣סְפ֔וּ שֹׂכֹ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר לִיהוּדָ֑ה וַֽיַּחֲנ֛וּ בֵּין־שׂוֹכֹ֥ה וּבֵין־עֲזֵקָ֖ה בְּאֶ֥פֶס דַּמִּֽים׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Καὶ συνάγουσιν ἀλλόφυλοι τὰς παρεμβολὰς αὐτῶν εἰς πόλεμον, καὶ συνάγονται εἰς Σοκχὼθ τῆς Ἰδουμαίας, καὶ παρεμβάλλουσιν ἀνὰ μέσον Σοκχὼθ καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον Ἀζηκὰ Ἐφερμέμ.

Douay-Rheims

Now the Philistines gathering together their troops to battle, assembled at Socho of Juda, and camped between Socho and Azeca in the borders of Dommim.

JPS (1917)

Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and they were gathered together at Socoh, which belongeth to Judah, and pitched between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Congregantes autem Philisthiim agmina sua in prælium, convenerunt in Socho Judæ: et castrametati sunt inter Socho et Azeca in finibus Dommim.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

وَجَمَعَ ٱلْفِلِسْطِينِيُّونَ جُيُوشَهُمْ لِلْحَرْبِ، فَٱجْتَمَعُوا فِي سُوكُوهَ ٱلَّتِي لِيَهُوذَا، وَنَزَلُوا بَيْنَ سُوكُوهَ وَعَزِيقَةَ فِي أَفَسِ دَمِّيمَ.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

JPS (1917)
